walkthroughs.body_html:
Religion & Ethics: Significant Concepts in Issues / Debates — a core area of A-Level Religious Studies.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Religion & Ethics: Significant Concepts in Issues / Debates brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Religion & Ethics: Significant Concepts in Issues / Debates.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: What does the concept of stewardship teach?
options: Humans should care for creation on God's behalf and are accountable for it
Humans may exploit nature without limit
Nature is divine and must never be touched
Only governments have environmental duties

mcqs.q: What did Lynn White famously argue in 1967?
options: That the Christian idea of dominion contributed to the ecological crisis
That religion invented environmentalism
That the environment cannot be damaged by humans
That deep ecology is a religious heresy
Nature has intrinsic value independent of its usefulness to humans
Nature matters only as a resource for people
Only endangered species have value
The environment is a human invention

mcqs.q: How does the idea of 'imago Dei' support equality?
options: All humans made in God's image share equal dignity and worth
Only religious believers have rights
Images of God must be displayed in public
Equality applies only to leaders

mcqs.q: Does 'dominion' in Genesis necessarily mean exploitation?
options: Dominion refers to a board game mentioned in Genesis.
Equality means everyone must hold the same beliefs.
No - many theologians read it as responsible rule in God's image, paired with Genesis 2:15's command to 'till and keep' the garden; exploitation is one contested interpretation.
The Bible simply commands humans to use up the natural world.

mcqs.q: Is concern for the environment a purely modern, secular invention?
options: Equality means everyone must hold the same beliefs.
Environmental ethics was first proposed in the year 2000.
Religions had nothing to say about the environment until secular movements forced them.
No - religious traditions contain long-standing resources, from sabbath rest for the land to Francis of Assisi, and modern statements such as the papal encyclical Laudato Si' (2015).

mcqs.q: Does equality mean treating everyone in exactly the same way?
options: Not necessarily - debates distinguish equal worth and rights from identical treatment; justice may require accommodating differences, such as disability access.
Environmental ethics was first proposed in the year 2000.
If people are equal, any difference in treatment is automatically unjust.
Equality means everyone must hold the same beliefs.
